title: How Living Heritage Teaches Us About Making a Policy
excerpt: Tepa Selira is more than empathy: it can inspire a policy stress test. Before a policy is implemented, compare its assumptions with other people's realities, deliberately invite divergent criticism, and test the edge cases before reality becomes the reviewer.
content:
What can living heritage teach us about making a policy? More than we might expect.

We often talk about living heritage as something we should preserve. But living heritage can also be read as a repository of social intelligence: ways communities have learned to coordinate, restrain themselves, solve collective problems, interpret conflict, and live with difference.

Take Tepa Selira.

At a basic level, Tepa Selira asks us to place ourselves in another person's position — to compare our own parameter with the possible experience of somebody else before we act. Existing literature on Tepa Selira links the value to cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of empathy, while the UNESCO framework for living heritage emphasises that communities who create, maintain and transmit heritage must participate in safeguarding and managing it.

The shift

If Tepa Selira asks a person to compare their own perspective with another person's reality, why not apply the same logic to policy design?

Part I — A Policy Is Also a Point of View

Every policy contains assumptions.

Who is the “normal” citizen?

What resources do we assume they have?

What information do we assume they can access?

How fast do we assume they can respond?

What language do we assume they understand?

What behaviour do we assume they will have?

What happens to the person who does not fit the average?

Policy teams often become extremely good at answering these questions without explicitly saying that they are making assumptions.

Then the policy is launched.

And suddenly the edge cases become real people.

Perhaps many policy failures are not failures of intelligence. They are failures of perspective.

Part II — Why Do Some Policies Produce Conflict Even When They Look Rational?

Here is my deliberately provocative question:

What if a policy causes conflict because nobody was assigned to make the policy uncomfortable before it was implemented?

A room full of competent people can still produce a fragile decision when everyone is solving the same problem using the same assumptions.

The danger is not that convergent thinking is bad. It is essential for narrowing options, applying standards and making decisions.

The danger is convergence without adversarial testing.

Imagine a policy process like this:

1. Define the problem
The team agrees on what the problem is.
2. Build the solution
The team develops an intervention that matches that definition.
3. Validate internally
The same people review the same assumptions.
4. Implement
Reality becomes the first serious stress test.

That last step is expensive.

Because once reality becomes the reviewer, the cost is no longer a workshop.

It can become budget loss, public resistance, implementation failure, staff burnout, legal disputes, damaged trust, or social conflict.

OECD guidance published in 2025 explicitly recommends stress-testing public policies against multiple plausible disruptions and using tools such as red teams, premortems and structured dissent to challenge assumptions before implementation. The same guidance cautions that evidence for red teaming in public administration remains limited, so it should be treated as a promising practice rather than a magic solution.

Part III — The “Annoying Critic” May Be an Institutional Sensor

Now we arrive at the uncomfortable part.

In many workplaces, the person who keeps asking:

“But what if…?”

can become unpopular.

“Why are you making this complicated?”

“We already decided.”

“That's not how we usually do it.”

“You're always finding problems.”

“You're too negative.”

Sometimes the critic really is simply being unhelpful. Criticism is not automatically insight.

But there is another possibility:

What if the person who keeps saying “but…” is functioning as a missing sensor in the organization?

A divergent thinker often expands the possibility space rather than immediately collapsing it into one answer. In a policy environment, that can look like criticism because the job is partly to expose alternatives, contradictions, hidden assumptions and edge cases.

That does not make the divergent thinker automatically right.

It makes their dissent potentially useful data.

Part IV — The Real Asset We Keep Throwing Away

Organizations frequently talk about “talent” as if talent were a list of qualifications.

Degree.

Certification.

Years of experience.

Test score.

Interview score.

KPI.

Those things can be useful evidence.

But they are still proxies.

The dangerous moment comes when the proxy becomes the definition of ability itself.

If the instrument cannot detect a capability, the capability can start to look like it does not exist.

This is especially important for people whose strengths are exploratory, connective, systems-oriented, unusual or difficult to standardise.

They may not “fit” a single job family.

They may produce ideas before the organization has a category for them.

They may jump between disciplines.

They may challenge the framing before accepting the task.

They may be irritating in meetings.

They may also be exactly the person who sees the failure mode nobody else saw.

Part V — “Divergent” Is a Thinking Mode, Not a Personality Ranking

This distinction matters.

I am not arguing that divergent people are better humans, better employees, or better policy makers.

Nor does “divergent” provide a clinical diagnosis or an excuse for poor behaviour.

The useful distinction is functional:

Convergent mode
Which option best satisfies the criteria?
Divergent mode
What possibilities, variables, stakeholders or consequences have not yet been considered?
Integration
Can we generate alternatives, stress-test them, and then converge on a defensible decision?

We need all three.

Because divergence without convergence can become chaos.

But convergence without divergence can become institutional blindness.

Part VI — Tepa Selira as a Cognitive Stress Test

This is where the cultural principle becomes surprisingly practical.

Suppose a ministry proposes a new service requirement.

The convergent question is:

“Does the procedure achieve the intended administrative objective?”

Tepa Selira adds another layer:

“How does this procedure behave when experienced by someone who has a very different set of constraints from ours?”

Then divergent thinking pushes further:

What if the assumption is wrong?

What if the average case is misleading?

What if the user cannot comply?

What if the policy creates a new incentive that nobody intended?

What if people adapt their behaviour around the rule?

What if the “exception” is actually a large but invisible group?

What happens after six months?

What happens when another disruption occurs at the same time?

Now the policy is no longer being evaluated only for whether it works in theory.

It is being tested for whether it survives contact with different realities.

Part VII — Why Critical Dissent Matters

There is a subtle organizational mistake here:

We sometimes treat disagreement as friction instead of treating disagreement as information.

A useful critical voice does not have to be rewarded simply because it is critical.

Instead, the organization can ask:

What assumption is being challenged?

What evidence would prove the criticism wrong?

What evidence would prove it right?

What edge case is being exposed?

Does the criticism reveal a design weakness?

That is the difference between argument and stress testing.

OECD's recent public-administration guidance describes red teams as arms-length collaborators who challenge assumptions, evidence and decision-making through structured dissent. It even suggests techniques such as checking explicit and implicit assumptions and systematically attempting to disconfirm competing hypotheses.

So perhaps the question is not “How do we silence the critic?” but “Can we convert criticism into a testable hypothesis?”

Part VIII — The Most Dangerous Sentence in Policy?

“We have already decided.”

Because that sentence can quietly transform evidence into decoration.

Once a team becomes psychologically committed to a solution, contradictory information becomes inconvenient.

And the divergent thinker becomes even more annoying.

Which is precisely why they may be useful.

The best time to hear “this could fail” is before failure becomes expensive.

Part IX — Living Heritage and the Anti-Top-Down Lesson

This is where UNESCO's living-heritage framework becomes directly relevant to policymaking.

The 2003 Convention calls for communities, groups and relevant organisations to participate in identifying living heritage, and Article 15 calls for the widest possible participation of the communities, groups and individuals who create, maintain and transmit it. UNESCO decisions concerning policies that may affect intangible cultural heritage also stress active participation and warn against top-down approaches.

That is not merely a heritage-management lesson.

It is a policy-design lesson:

The people affected by a system are not merely “beneficiaries.” They are potential sources of intelligence about whether the system will work.

The community knows the loophole the policy designer never imagined.

The frontline worker knows where the workflow breaks.

The local practitioner knows what the spreadsheet cannot see.

The unusual employee knows which assumption everyone has quietly normalised.

The critic knows which sentence makes the whole thing uncomfortable.

And discomfort can be useful.

Part X — The Black Death / Cats Story: A Warning About the Metaphor

There is a famous story that Europe killed cats and thereby helped rats spread the Black Death.

It is a great metaphor.

It is also a poor historical fact to repeat without qualification. The popular story simplifies a much more complicated history, and the causal claim that mass cat killing drove the plague is disputed.

So I would use the story differently:

Imagine a society destroying a potentially useful asset simply because its value was invisible to the dominant belief system.

That mechanism is entirely plausible inside modern institutions.

We can discard a person because their value is not visible to our test.

We can discard a warning because it does not fit our narrative.

We can discard local knowledge because it does not look like formal expertise.

We can discard a critic because they are irritating.

And afterwards, we wonder why the system became less resilient.

Part XI — Google Is Actually a Useful Counterexample

And yes: Google is not a clean example of “one narrow test decides everything.”

Google has publicly described structured interviews, consistent evaluation criteria and efforts to reduce bias in hiring. Google has also described project-based assessments designed around real-world engineering work, rather than relying only on abstract technical puzzles.

That matters because the argument here should not become:

“All organizations are convergent and all tests are bad.”

That would itself be a convergent stereotype.

The stronger argument is:

Every organization should examine what its measurement system systematically makes visible — and what it systematically makes invisible.

Google is therefore a useful reminder that organizations can design broader assessment systems.

Part XII — A Better Architecture: Diverge → Stress-Test → Converge

Diverge. Expand the space of possibilities.

Stress-test. Invite structured dissent. Attack assumptions, not people.

Converge. Make the decision using evidence, explicit criteria and accountability.

Then repeat.

This resembles the logic of strategic foresight: explore disruptions, imagine interactions, build scenarios, test strategies and identify actions that remain robust across multiple possible futures.

Part XIII — So What Does Tepa Selira Actually Teach a Policymaker?

The policy translation

“Before I impose my parameter on society, I should test what happens when society does not share my parameter.”

That is Tepa Selira translated into policy language.

Not “be nice.”

Not “never disagree.”

Not “all perspectives are equally correct.”

Something much more operational:

Never confuse the parameter used to measure reality with reality itself.

Part XIV — The Provocation

So here is the question I would leave with policymakers, managers, recruiters and anyone who designs systems:

How many valuable people have we called “difficult” because our organization had no instrument for measuring what they were actually good at?
How many policies have failed because the only people allowed to validate them were the same people who designed them?
How many conflicts could have been prevented if someone had been paid to disagree before implementation rather than blamed for complaining afterwards?
And how many “exceptions” are actually signals that our definition of normal is too narrow?

Maybe the goal is not to make every person more convergent.

Maybe the goal is to build organizations that know when to converge and when to deliberately diverge.

Because a system without convergence cannot decide.

But a system without divergence cannot see what it is missing.

And a system without Tepa Selira may make a perfectly rational decision — from the wrong person's point of view.

One final thought

A critic is not automatically right. But an institution that never listens to critics may eventually discover that it has removed one of its own warning systems.

Living heritage is not only about remembering how people lived.

Sometimes it teaches us how systems should listen before they decide.

Key References & Reading

1. UNESCO — 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage
Community participation, national policy measures, and Article 15 on active involvement in safeguarding and management.
2. UNESCO — About Living Heritage and Education
Living heritage is community-based; communities are central to its creation, maintenance and transmission.
3. UNESCO — Decision 10.COM 14.a
Policies and programmes that affect living heritage should involve the communities concerned and respect ethical considerations.
4. Hamidah et al. (2026) — Tepa Selira and empathy
Systematic literature review connecting Tepa Selira with cognitive, affective and behavioural dimensions of empathy.
5. OECD — Behavioural Science in the Italian Public Administration
Pre-mortems, calibrated forecasting and red teams as practices for challenging assumptions and stress-testing public decisions.
6. OECD — Strategic Foresight Toolkit for Resilient Public Policy
A five-module process for exploring disruptions, building scenarios and stress-testing policies across possible futures.
7. Google — Structured decision-making and hiring
Google's public discussion of structured interviews and consistent evaluation criteria.
8. Google / Byteboard — Work-sample assessment
Project-based assessment designed around real-world engineering skills.
9. Historical caveat on the cat / Black Death story

The popular claim that mass cat killing caused the Black Death by increasing rats is disputed and should not be presented as settled history. In this article the story is used only as a metaphor for the broader risk of discarding assets whose value a dominant measurement system cannot see.

title: When Effort Changes the Choice: An Analogy Between Relationships and Diplomacy
excerpt: Why two options with similar baseline value can lead to different choices once trust, damage, effort, repair and opportunity cost enter the picture—and how the same logic can be used as a diplomatic analogy.
content:
Consider this simple situation. You have two options, A and B. They are equally attractive. Then A hurts you, while B does not. Later, both approach you. All else being equal, why would you not prefer B?

Now change one variable: A makes a serious effort to repair the damage. A shows up, changes behaviour, sacrifices time, accepts a commitment that was previously resisted, and consistently demonstrates that the relationship matters. Suddenly, A is no longer the same option you evaluated at the moment of the original injury.

The intuition is not really about beauty. It is about accumulated value.

Two people can begin with similar baseline value. Their subsequent choices change the history of the relationship. One person may create trust, the other may create damage. One may invest effort, the other may remain passive. The eventual choice is therefore not based only on what each person was at the beginning, but also on what interacting with each person has become.

That is the analogy I want to explore here. It is useful in relationships, but it can also be used as a way of thinking about diplomacy, negotiation and institutional relationships.

1. The relationship thought experiment

Start with the cleanest case.

A and B are equally attractive. A hurts you. B does not. A and B both later express interest.

A = baseline 8 − damage 3 = 5 B = baseline 8 + stable history 0 = 8

In this simplified model, B has an advantage. Not because B became more beautiful, richer or more impressive, but because the interaction history is different.

Now suppose A begins to invest.

A = baseline 8 − damage 3 + repair effort 4 = 9 B = baseline 8 = 8

Now A can become competitive again.

That does not mean that every hurt can be repaired by enough effort. Some actions change the decision boundary permanently. Some people will not want to continue even after a sincere apology. Consent, boundaries and personal values remain decisive. The calculation is therefore a thought experiment: it shows why a choice can change when the inputs change.

Effort does not erase history. It changes what the history means for the next decision.

2. “A + effort” is not the same as “A says sorry”

This is where the idea becomes more interesting.

Effort has levels. It is not a binary variable where someone either “tries” or “doesn't try.”

LevelRelationship exampleWhat it signals
Presencekeeping company, replying, showing upattention
Timerearranging a schedule, making roomopportunity cost
Practical sacrificehelping with something inconvenient or difficultinvestment
Behavioural changechanging a habit that repeatedly caused conflictlearning
Future commitmentchanging a major life decision because the relationship matterslong-term cost
Consistent repairacknowledgement + corrective action + sustained consistencycredibility

This is why a person can say, “I already made an effort,” while the other person still experiences no meaningful repair. The two people may be assigning different values to the same action.

For example, spending ten minutes sending a message may be effort. Changing a long-term plan can also be effort. They are both effort, but their opportunity costs are different.

3. The commitment example

Consider a very specific example: someone initially does not want marriage, while the other person wants marriage. Later, the first person decides to marry because the relationship itself has become sufficiently valuable to justify a major change of plan.

That decision is more than a romantic sentence. It is a costly commitment.

In the model, the relevant point is not “marriage is always the correct repair.” It is that changing a major prior decision carries a larger opportunity cost than simply saying, “I am sorry.”

Important distinction: effort should never be treated as entitlement. A large sacrifice does not create ownership over another person. It is simply evidence about what someone is willing to invest.

4. The surprising case: B is less attractive, but B invests

Now make the baseline values different.

A is very attractive: baseline 9.

B is more ordinary: baseline 6.

Yet B provides meaningful effort, consistency and trust.

A = 9 + 0 = 9 B = 6 + 3 = 9

The two options can become comparable.

This is a useful reminder that people do not necessarily optimise a single attribute. Physical attractiveness can be important, but so can reliability, treatment, compatibility, trust, shared goals and the cost of maintaining the relationship.

Now reverse the situation.

B has the lower baseline, then hurts you, then provides no repair effort.

A = 9 + effort 2 = 11 B = 6 − damage 3 + effort 0 = 3

In the simplified model, there is no reason to assume B remains competitive merely because B was previously chosen or previously available.

The option with the highest starting value does not always win. But a lower starting value also does not automatically disappear. What matters is the accumulated position after interaction, effort, damage and cost are considered.

5. The same logic appears in diplomacy

Now translate the thought experiment into international relations.

Imagine a state says something damaging about another state. Perhaps the statement is inaccurate, provocative, careless or simply misunderstood. Regardless of intent, the other side can now incorporate that event into its assessment of the relationship.

The analogy is not that governments literally “choose the prettier person.” The analogy is that relationships accumulate history.

A diplomatic partner may be evaluated on:

Strategic value
What does cooperation provide?
Trust
Can commitments be relied upon?
Friction
How difficult is cooperation?
Reputation
What signal does this behaviour send?
Reciprocity
Does cooperation tend to be returned?
Risk
What additional uncertainty is created?

That makes a diplomatic blunder conceptually similar to damage in a relationship.

Net Diplomatic Position = Interest + Trust + Cooperation Value + Repair Effort − Damage − Friction − Risk

6. The Suez Canal thought experiment — and the important caveat

Suppose, purely as a hypothetical example, State A and State B both seek the same type of access or cooperation. State A has just created a diplomatic problem with another country by making an inaccurate or sensitive statement. State B has not.

The intuitive question is: “Would the damaged relationship create extra friction?”

Possibly—but the actual Suez Canal case cannot be reduced to personal preference. The Suez Canal Authority states that transit is available to vessels of all nations subject to the rules of navigation, and the Constantinople Convention establishes a principle of free use of the canal under its terms. The SCA also states that it should not discriminate between comparable users in conflict with those rules. citeturn141755search1turn141755search0turn141755search4

So the diplomatic analogy should be read this way:

A damaged bilateral relationship may create political or diplomatic friction around a request, but it does not replace the legal and institutional rules governing an international transit system.

That distinction is crucial. The model is about relationship dynamics, not a claim that diplomatic feelings can simply override law or operating rules.

7. The broker scenario: “Let me help bring you closer”

There is another pattern.

Someone says:

“Come on. I can help connect you with them. Let's cooperate.”

The other side agrees. The broker begins creating access, trust and coordination.

Then the broker makes a careless statement.

Maybe it is intentional. Maybe accidental. Maybe the wording is simply misunderstood.

Now the broker's value proposition has changed.

Broker Value = Access Created + Trust Built − Miscommunication − Repair Cost

This is why diplomatic relationships often require more than saying, “That was not what I meant.” The broker or intermediary may need clarification, correction, reassurance, a new proposal, additional transparency or a concrete action that restores confidence.

In other words, the worse the damage, the more credible the repair usually has to be.

8. Simulation: change the assumptions and watch the choice move

The simulation below is intentionally simple. It is not a psychological test and it is not a diplomatic prediction engine. It is a transparent way to see the logic of the analogy.

Option A

B is ahead under the current assumptions.

B starts from the same baseline but has more positive relational inputs and less damage.

How to read the simulation

Move one slider at a time. Notice that a lower-baseline option can become competitive when effort and trust rise. Also notice the reverse: a high-baseline option can lose its advantage when damage, friction or ongoing cost become large.

The model uses:

Final Score = Baseline + Effort + Trust − Damage − Cost

For the diplomacy mode, interpret “baseline” as strategic or cooperation value, “trust” as relationship capital, “effort” as confidence-building or repair, “damage” as diplomatic friction/reputational cost, and “cost” as operational or political risk.

9. What this model explains — and what it does not

It explains trade-offs.
A lower starting value can be offset by meaningful effort under some assumptions.
It explains repair.
Damage changes the starting point for the next decision; repair changes that position again.
It explains why history matters.
Two otherwise similar options may not remain equivalent after different interactions.
It does not predict people.
Humans can reject an option despite a high score because values, boundaries and emotions are not fully captured here.

10. The deeper analogy

The deeper idea is not “beauty versus effort.” It is relative value under relationship history.

Imagine two suppliers. One has excellent technical capability but repeatedly creates friction. Another is slightly less capable but reliable, responsive and cooperative. A procurement decision may look different once transaction costs and reliability are included.

Imagine two organizations seeking a partnership. One has strong resources but has recently created avoidable trust problems. The other has fewer resources but a stronger history of cooperation. Again, the decision is not only about the initial asset base.

Imagine a diplomatic intermediary who promises to make cooperation easier. The intermediary can increase value by creating access and confidence. But a careless statement can destroy part of that value and trigger repair costs.

Across all three cases, the same structure appears:

Starting Value → Interaction → Trust / Damage → Effort / Repair → Revised Value → New Choice

The sequence is dynamic. That is the important part.

11. The idea of “A + effort” in one sentence

A person, organization or state can become a different option in the decision-maker's eyes because the relationship history has changed—not because its original characteristics suddenly changed.

That is why “A was better on paper” and “B was chosen” are not necessarily contradictory.

The paper may describe the baseline.

The relationship describes what happened after the baseline.

12. Closing: value is not static

So perhaps the real lesson is this:

When two options begin with comparable value, the way they treat you can become part of the value calculation.

Effort can add value.

Trust can add value.

Damage can subtract value.

Repair can restore part of what was lost.

And large commitments can matter precisely because they carry opportunity costs.

This is also why the analogy with diplomacy is useful—but only up to the point where legal rules, institutions, strategic interests and other constraints take over. In relationships, no formula can override consent. In diplomacy, no informal “relationship score” overrides treaty obligations or formal navigation rules.

The useful question is therefore not “Who is objectively better?” It is: “Given the history, the costs, the effort and the constraints, how has the relative value of these options changed?”

This article is a conceptual framework and simulation developed to make the intuition visible. The scores are illustrative, not empirically calibrated measures of human attraction, trust, or state behaviour.
